title: Motion in a Straight Line — NIOS Official Summary
intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Physics (312) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 2: Motion in a Straight Line. It covers distance and displacement, speed and velocity, relative velocity, acceleration, position-time and velocity-time graphs, the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion, and motion under gravity.

branches.label: Distance & Displacement
details: Displacement is the shortest distance with direction

branches.label: Speed & Velocity
details: Speed: rate of change of distance
Velocity: rate of change of displacement

branches.label: Acceleration
details: Time rate of change of velocity

sections.heading: Distance, Displacement, Speed and Velocity
bullets: The total length of the path covered by a body is the distance travelled by it.
The difference between the initial and final position vectors of a body is called its displacement.
Displacement is the shortest distance between the two positions and has a certain direction.
The rate of change of distance with time is called speed.
The rate of change of displacement is known as velocity.

sections.heading: Average Velocity and Average Speed
bullets: The average velocity of an object is defined as the displacement per unit time: v̄ = displacement / time taken = (x₂ − x₁) / (t₂ − t₁).
The average speed of an object is obtained by dividing the total distance travelled by the total time taken.
Average speed and the magnitude of average velocity are equal only when motion is in a single direction without reversal.

sections.heading: Relative Velocity
bullets: The relative velocity of an object with respect to another object is the rate at which it changes its position relative to the reference object.
The rate of change of the relative position of an object with respect to the other object is known as the relative velocity of that object with respect to the other.
The relative velocity of B with respect to A is v_B − v_A.

sections.heading: Acceleration
bullets: Acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of velocity.
Acceleration is a vector quantity and its SI unit is m s⁻².
Average acceleration ā = (final velocity − initial velocity) / time taken = (v₂ − v₁) / (t₂ − t₁).
The decrease in the rate of change of velocity (deceleration) is called retardation.

sections.heading: Motion Graphs
bullets: Position-Time Graph: the different positions and corresponding times can be plotted on a graph (time along x-axis, position along y-axis).
A motion in which the velocity of the moving object is constant is known as uniform motion.
If the distances covered in successive equal time intervals are increasing, the motion is accelerated motion (non-uniform).
Instantaneous velocity: the velocity of the particle at any instant of time is v = Δx/Δt — the slope of a line tangent to the position-time curve at that point.
Velocity-Time Graph: in uniform motion the velocity is constant; in non-uniform motion, the slope (Δv/Δt) gives the acceleration.
Distance travelled = area of trapezium under the v-t graph = ½ × (v₁ + v₂) × (t₂ − t₁).

sections.heading: Equations of Uniformly Accelerated Motion
bullets: First equation: v = v₀ + at, derived from a = (final velocity − initial velocity) / time.
Second equation: x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², derived from x − x₀ = (1/2)(v + v₀)t and substitution of v = v₀ + at.
Third equation: v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀), derived by eliminating t between the first two equations.
These equations are valid only when the acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction.

sections.heading: Motion under Gravity
bullets: The free fall of a body towards the earth is one of the most common examples of motion with constant acceleration.
Replacing a by g in the equations of motion: v = v₀ + gt; x = x₀ + v₀t + ½gt²; v² = v₀² + 2g(x − x₀).
g is the acceleration due to gravity (≈ 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface), directed vertically downward.

key_takeaways: Distance is the scalar path length; displacement is the vector change in position — distance ≥ |displacement| always.
Speed is the rate of change of distance (scalar); velocity is the rate of change of displacement (vector).
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (a vector, SI unit m/s²); retardation is negative acceleration.
The slope of an x-t graph gives velocity; the slope of a v-t graph gives acceleration; the area under a v-t graph gives displacement.
The three equations of motion v = v₀ + at, x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² and v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀) apply only when acceleration is constant.
Free fall is the special case with a = g downward.

glossary.definition: The total length of the path covered by a moving body — a scalar quantity, always non-negative.
The difference between the initial and final position vectors of a body — the shortest distance between the two positions, with a specific direction. A vector quantity.
The rate of change of distance with time. A scalar quantity that is always non-negative.
The rate of change of displacement. A vector quantity with both magnitude and direction.
The displacement of an object divided by the time taken: v̄ = (x₂ − x₁) / (t₂ − t₁).
The velocity of a particle at a specific instant of time, equal to the slope of the tangent to the position-time curve at that point.
The time rate of change of velocity; a vector quantity with SI unit m s⁻².
A decrease in the rate of change of velocity (i.e. negative acceleration in the direction of motion).
Motion in which the velocity of the moving body is constant — the position-time graph is a straight line with constant slope.
Motion of a body under gravity alone, with constant downward acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface.
